title: Stairwell dry removal and damp cleaning
audience: Cleaners who service shared stairwells in offices, apartment buildings and commercial sites.
learningOutcomes: Choose between a backpack vacuum and a dust mop for dry soil on steps and landings.
Damp clean steps and landings using a flat mop pad, moving from the top down and keeping a clear exit.
Manage the work area so that no one is at risk of a slip or fall on a wet tread.

instruction.heading: Stairs carry soil in a different way
instruction.body: Stairwells collect grit, leaves and dust on the treads and the landing edges, and the nosing of each step is where most of it sits. Dry soil on steps is best taken up before any wet work, so that the damp pad does not turn it into a film. The main safety issue is that stairs are used on the move, so the cleaning must be arranged so people can still pass safely while the work is done.

instruction.heading: Dry removal: vacuum first, dust mop as the fallback
instruction.body: A backpack vacuum is the quickest tool for dry soil on stairs, because the wand reaches the nosing of each tread. Where a backpack is not available, a dust mop can do the job, but it is slower. With either tool, work from the top landing down. For a vacuum, set the nozzle at the outer edge of each tread and sweep across to the far side before stepping up. For a dust mop, walk the head across each tread in a steady motion, keeping the head on the surface, and gather the soil into a pile on the landing.

instruction.heading: Damp cleaning using a flat mop
instruction.body: After the dry work, set out a wet floor sign by each entrance to the stairwell and lay one clean, damp pad on every landing, drawn out of the charging bucket. Carry a small liner in a back pocket for used pads. Start on the top landing, mopping the corners and edges and then the open area. Then work down the flight standing on a finished tread, reach the next tread with the damp pad, drawing it across the width and then toward the nosing. Swap the dirty pad for the clean one waiting on the landing, and drop the dirty pad into the liner. Pass the liner down to the following landing, and repeat until the base is reached.

instruction.heading: Finishing the stairwell
instruction.body: Once the stairwell is complete and the treads and landings are dry, remove the signs from the entrances. Carry the flat mop and bucket back to storage, put the soiled pads in the laundry basket, then rinse and dry the bucket before storing it. Check the nosings and the handrails for any remaining film, and report a persistent film to the supervisor.

procedure: Put on gloves and eye protection, and check the steps and landings for loose debris or spills.
Clear the landings of mats and set out a wet floor sign by each entrance.
Dry-clean with a backpack vacuum, working each tread from one end to the other as you descend.
If no backpack vacuum is available, run a dust mop with steady passes, keeping the head on the surface, and gather soil into a pile on every landing.
Lay a damp pad on every landing and carry a small liner for used pads.
Starting at the top landing, mop the corners and edges, then the open area, moving down the stairs.
On each tread, draw the damp pad across its width, then toward the nosing.
Replace the dirty pad on every landing, bag it in the can liner, and send the liner down to the following landing.
Return the equipment to the closet, and remove the signs once the stairs are dry.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner damp mops a stairwell from the bottom up and leaves a wet film on the treads that a resident slips on as they come down.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the cleaner have done differently?
workedExamples.reasoning: Work from the top down so the cleaner is never working below a wet surface that people must use, and set out wet floor signs by both ends. Dry-clean first so grit is not smeared into a film. If the film is already there, put a sign up at once and report it.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner has no backpack vacuum for a stairwell and decides on a dust mop with long, fast strokes that lift the head at the end of each tread.
workedExamples.reasoning: Keep the head on the surface and use steady, controlled passes, then gather the soil into a pile on the landing. Lifting and swinging the head sends dust back into the air and onto the treads already done.

equipmentAndPpe: Back-pack vacuum with a long wand and a flat-tread tool, or a dust mop.
Extension cord, where the vacuum needs power from a marked outlet.
Flat mop with clean microfiber pads, and a charging bucket.
Small can liner for dirty pads.
Dust pan and broom for gathering soil on landings.
Wet floor signs for both entrances.

commonErrors.error: Mopping from the bottom up, so the cleaner stands on wet treads and people must walk through the wet work.
commonErrors.prevention: Work from the top landing down, and keep a sign at each entrance.

commonErrors.error: Damp mopping without removing the dry soil first, which turns grit into a film.
commonErrors.prevention: Dry-clean the treads first, then damp mop.

commonErrors.error: Leaving the cord across a tread or at the handrail, where it can catch a foot.
commonErrors.prevention: Run the cord between the handrails and move it to the next outlet before it becomes a trip hazard.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Keep people off the stairs while they are wet, and mark both ends with signs. Never leave a wet tread unmarked.
Check the vacuum cord for cuts or damage before use. Do not use a cord with a missing earth pin, and report it instead.
Use both hands on handrails when moving up or down with equipment. Do not carry a bucket and a vacuum simultaneously on the stairs.

qualityStandard: Dry soil is removed from every tread and landing, including the nosings.
Each landing and tread is damp cleaned without a visible film once dry.
Signs are in place at both ends while the stairs are wet, and removed once dry.
The cord is stowed clear of the handrails and the treads.
No dirty pad or can liner is left on a landing.
documentationEvidence: Job record of the stairwell cleaned, with the date, time and floors covered.
Note of any damaged tread, handrail, or any film that did not clear, for supervisor review.
summary: Remove dry soil first with a backpack vacuum, or a dust mop where no vacuum is available.
Damp clean from the top down, one tread at a time, replacing dirty pads as you go.
Mark both entrances while the stairs are wet, and keep the route clear.
Report any persistent film or damaged step.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which direction should stairs be cleaned in, and why?
options: From the bottom up, so the dirt falls toward the top landing and the bottom stays clean
From the top down, so the cleaner never works below a wet surface people must use
From the middle outward in both directions at once and the landings last

knowledgeChecks.question: What should happen before damp mopping a stairwell?
options: The treads are flooded with cleaner so the grit lifts
Every tread is coated with polish to hold the soil
Dry soil is removed first, usually with a backpack vacuum

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a dirty pad be placed in a can liner rather than dropped on the stairs?
options: So that the soil stays contained and is not spread onto the treads
So that the pad can be reused without washing it on the next stair
So that the pad dries faster on the landing before the next stair
